source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture (អគ្គនាយកដ្ឋានកសិកម្ម), Department of Rice Crop (នាយកដ្ឋានដំណាំស្រូវ) — "Post-Harvest Rice Technology Handbook" (សៀវភៅបច្ចេកទេសក្រោយប្រមូលផលស្រូវ), June 2014, produced with support from an ADB grant (ADB Grant No. 0302 Cam-EF). No elibrary.maff.gov.kh URL is visible on the scanned pages provided, so none is given here — confirm the source link if this file is later cross-checked against the online elibrary.
text: The source outlines a formal seed multiplication and certification hierarchy commonly used in the region: Breeder seed (ពូជដើមកំណើត) is multiplied to produce Foundation seed (ពូជគ្រឹះ), which is multiplied to produce Registered seed (ពូជចុះបញ្ជី), which is multiplied to produce Certified seed (ពូជបញ្ជាក់/ពូជទទួលស្គាល់) — the grade typically sold to farmers for planting their main crop. Quality requirements are strictest at the Breeder/Foundation end and loosen slightly at Registered/Certified level while still requiring high purity throughout. Illustrative benchmark figures given in the source's comparison tables include: pure seed content around 98% across all grades; other-variety seed contamination held at essentially zero for Breeder/Foundation seed, with small allowances (on the order of a few seeds per unit weight) permitted at Registered/Certified level; weed seed content capped at roughly 2%; noxious or red rice seed kept near zero at the higher grades with a small allowance at Registered/Certified level; a minimum germination rate around 80%; and a maximum moisture content around 14% for all grades. A separate table in the source compares similarly strict tolerances used in a neighboring country's certification system, generally in the range of a few tenths of a percent for various contaminant categories (other-variety seed, weed seed, inert matter) depending on the grade. For a farmer choosing seed, the practical takeaway is that higher-grade certified seed costs more but comes with fewer off-type plants, more even maturity, and better germination — generally worth prioritizing for the main crop, even where home-saved or lower-grade seed is used for less critical or smaller plantings. (Note: the specific percentage thresholds here are illustrative figures drawn from the source's tables; farmers or input suppliers relying on formal seed grading should confirm current official standards with Cambodia's seed certification authority rather than treating these numbers as binding.)
